notes:
Task and constraints: Find the smallest number on a card that can appear on only one side after flipping.
Idea: Collect numbers that appear identically on both sides, then choose the smallest other visible value.
Technique and why it applies: Any number equal on both sides can never be hidden, so it is excluded from the candidate values.
Invariant: The set of equal front-back values is the forbidden set.
Edge cases: If every number is forbidden, the code returns zero as required; duplicates do not change eligibility.
Complexity: Building sets and scanning all card values takes O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the smallest eligible number after flipping any cards.
Idea: Build the set of values equal on both sides, then scan both arrays for the smallest value outside it.
Technique and why it applies: A number printed on both sides of one card can never be hidden; all other values can be made visible without that blocker.
Invariant: same contains forbidden values and result tracks the minimum eligible value.
Edge cases: If no eligible value exists, infinity is converted to zero. The arrays are assumed to have equal lengths.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Count binary trees whose nodes are values from nums and each parent equals the product of its children.
Idea: Memoize the number of trees rooted at each value, trying every factor pair present in the set.
Technique and why it applies: Each valid ordered factor pair contributes the product of possible left and right subtrees, plus the single-node tree.
Invariant: helper(num) returns the number of trees rooted at num.
Edge cases: lru_cache is used without an import in the snippet. Iterating both factor orders counts left-right-swapped trees separately as required by the problem.
Complexity: Runtime is roughly O(n²) factor checks with memoized states; space is O(n) plus recursion.

Task and constraints: Count binary trees where each non-leaf node equals the product of its children.
Idea: Sort values and compute ways for each root using smaller factors already processed.
Technique and why it applies: For every divisor A[j], if the complementary factor exists in dp, multiply the subtree counts and add them to the root count.
Invariant: dp[x] stores the number of trees rooted at value x, modulo 10^9+7.
Edge cases: The input is mutated by sorting. Distinct positive values are assumed by the task.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(n²) expected time and O(n) DP space.

Task and constraints: Convert each word in a sentence to Goat Latin.
Idea: Split on spaces, preserve each word's vowel or consonant rule, then append ma and an increasing run of a characters.
Technique and why it applies: Vowel-leading words stay in place; other words move their first character to the end before the suffix is added.
Invariant: index tracks the one-based word position and controls the number of appended a characters.
Edge cases: split(' ') preserves empty tokens from repeated spaces, which can cause word[0] to fail on malformed spacing; normal input uses single spaces.
Complexity: The work is O(total sentence length plus suffix output) and output storage is linear.

Task and constraints: Convert a sentence to Goat Latin while preserving word order.
Idea: Split into words, rotate consonant-leading words, and generate each transformed word with its indexed suffix.
Technique and why it applies: The generator adds ma followed by i copies of a, where i starts at one.
Invariant: Each yielded word is its completed Goat Latin form.
Edge cases: split() collapses repeated whitespace, unlike split(' '); the standard sentence constraints use ordinary spaces.
Complexity: Time and output space are O(total transformed sentence length).

Task and constraints: Count friend requests under the specified age restrictions.
Idea: Count each age and sum eligible ordered sender-recipient pairs using frequency multiplication.
Technique and why it applies: request implements the allowed age interval; equal-age pairs subtract one to exclude a person requesting themselves.
Invariant: c stores the frequency of every age and each term counts valid directed requests for an age pair.
Edge cases: The formula uses the exact rule 0.5*a+7 < b <= a. Ages violating it contribute zero.
Complexity: With U distinct ages, time is O(U²+n) and counter space is O(U).

Task and constraints: Maximize total profit by assigning each worker one job they can perform.
Idea: Sort jobs by difficulty, store prefix maximum profit, and binary-search the best feasible job for each worker.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix maxima ensure the searched job's profit represents the best job among all jobs no harder than that job.
Invariant: arr is sorted by difficulty and each profit slot becomes the best profit through that position.
Edge cases: The snippet uses inf without importing it, so execution fails unless inf is defined externally. Workers unable to do any job earn zero.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), workers cost O(m log n), and space is O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the largest island after changing at most one water cell into land.
Idea: Union adjacent land cells, storing component sizes, then evaluate each water cell by summing unique neighboring components.
Technique and why it applies: Flipping a water cell connects all distinct adjacent islands plus the new cell.
Invariant: parent identifies DSU roots and rank stores component sizes despite its name.
Edge cases: The index calculation uses i*m+j instead of i*n+j; it is wrong for non-square grids. The grid is assumed nonempty.
Complexity: DSU processing is near O(RC α(RC)) time and O(RC) space.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum island area obtainable by flipping one zero to one.
Idea: DFS labels each existing island with a unique index and records its area, then tests each zero cell.
Technique and why it applies: A flipped cell joins neighboring islands with distinct labels, so their areas are summed once plus one.
Invariant: area maps island labels to sizes; labels greater than one identify visited land components.
Edge cases: If the grid is all land, the largest existing area is returned. The method mutates grid by labeling islands.
Complexity: The grid is traversed a constant number of times, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) space.

Task and constraints: Sum the number of substrings in which each character appears exactly once.
Idea: Record every index for each character, then sum its contribution using gaps to neighboring occurrences.
Technique and why it applies: For each occurrence, left choices times right choices counts substrings where that occurrence is the unique instance of its character.
Invariant: idx_recorder maps each character to sorted occurrence positions; helper sums contributions for one character.
Edge cases: collections is referenced without an import in the snippet, so it needs external definition. The final sum counts all unique-character contributions.
Complexity: The occurrence scans take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Count unique-character contributions across all substrings modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Track the previous two occurrence positions for each uppercase character and add each occurrence's contribution.
Technique and why it applies: For occurrence i, the number of substrings where it is unique equals the distance to the previous occurrence times the distance to the next occurrence; the final pass closes suffixes.
Invariant: index[c] stores the two latest positions for each character.
Edge cases: The code assumes uppercase English letters because the dictionary uses ascii_uppercase; other characters would cause a key error.
Complexity: One scan plus a final alphabet pass takes O(n) time and O(1) alphabet-sized space.

Task and constraints: Count ways to represent n as a sum of consecutive positive integers.
Idea: Try each possible sequence length and use the sum of preceding integers to test divisibility.
Technique and why it applies: A length-i sequence beginning at a positive integer has a fixed offset sum; the remainder must divide evenly by i.
Invariant: csum tracks the offset 0+1+...+(i-1), and result counts valid lengths.
Edge cases: The loop stops once csum reaches n, and positive n is assumed.
Complexity: The loop takes O(n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Return the start and end indices of runs of at least three identical characters.
Idea: Scan characters while tracking the current run length and previous character.
Technique and why it applies: When the character changes, a qualifying previous run is emitted; a special last-character check handles a run ending at the string boundary.
Invariant: prev and c represent the current run's character and length.
Edge cases: The bitwise & is used instead of and in the final-position condition; both operands are booleans here, so the intended check still works.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(number of groups) output space.

Task and constraints: Find all intervals containing at least three consecutive equal characters.
Idea: Scan until a character differs or the string ends, then record the run if its length is at least three.
Technique and why it applies: The run boundaries are start i and current endpoint j; advancing i begins the next run.
Invariant: i marks the current run's start and j advances through the string.
Edge cases: The final index is handled in the same branch as a character change, so trailing large groups are not missed.
Complexity: The scan takes O(n) time and O(g) output space for g groups.

Task and constraints: Mask an email address or phone number according to privacy rules.
Idea: For emails, lowercase the first and last local-part letters and mask the middle; otherwise scan phone digits from right to left.
Technique and why it applies: The phone branch ignores formatting symbols, reveals the last four digits, and adds a country-code mask based on remaining digit count.
Invariant: flag switches from revealed digits to masked digits, while c counts remaining country-code digits.
Edge cases: Email parsing assumes exactly two domain labels, so multi-part domains are truncated. Phone formatting logic depends on its constructed string length.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and O(n) output space.

Task and constraints: Flip each row horizontally and invert every binary pixel.
Idea: Reverse each row and map each bit to one minus itself.
Technique and why it applies: Horizontal reversal changes column order, and subtraction from one flips zero to one and one to zero.
Invariant: The comprehension creates a new row for each original row and a new image.
Edge cases: The original image is not mutated; rows are assumed to contain only binary values.
Complexity: Time is O(RC) and output space is O(RC).

Task and constraints: Flip each row horizontally and invert its binary values in place.
Idea: Swap mirrored elements while XORing each bit with one.
Technique and why it applies: For each symmetric pair, the assignments reverse positions and invert both values; the middle element of an odd row is inverted once.
Invariant: Each processed pair is written into its mirrored positions in the same row.
Edge cases: The input image is mutated and returned. Python's simultaneous assignment evaluates both right-hand sides before writes.
Complexity: The method takes O(RC) time and O(1) extra space.

Task and constraints: Apply multiple find-and-replace operations at their original indices when source text matches.
Idea: Sort operations by index, track a cumulative offset, and perform each replacement on the changing string.
Technique and why it applies: The offset adjusts later original indices for length changes from earlier replacements.
Invariant: offset is the net length change introduced by accepted earlier operations.
Edge cases: The method prints debug output when a source fails to match. Correctness assumes operation indices are distinct and sorted processing matches the problem rules.
Complexity: Repeated string slicing can make runtime O(nm) for m operations and O(n) working space.

Task and constraints: Apply replacements at original indices only when each source substring matches.
Idea: Process operations in descending index order so edits to the right do not shift positions to the left.
Technique and why it applies: Each matching source is replaced directly; descending order preserves the original indices of all unprocessed operations.
Invariant: S is the current string after replacements at larger positions have been applied.
Edge cases: The method assumes replacement indices are valid and can be sorted independently; it does not mutate the caller's immutable string.
Complexity: Each replacement may copy O(n) characters, giving O(mn) worst-case time and O(n) space.
